title: The brain's resident immune cells
objective: Describe microglia, their unusual origin, and why the CNS has its own immune cells.

steps.title: Immune cells that live in the brain
steps.body:
The CNS sits behind the blood-brain barrier, so it keeps its own resident immune cells: **[[microglia]]**. They are the brain's main innate immune cell, a specialized macrophage-like population (B1-L3).

They monitor the tissue, respond to damage and infection, and shape circuits in development.

steps.title: An unusual origin
steps.body:
Most immune cells come from bone marrow in adulthood. Microglia are different: fate-mapping (2010) showed they arise from **primitive (yolk-sac) macrophages** early in development and then largely **self-renew** in place.

So microglia are a long-lived, brain-resident lineage, not constantly replaced from the blood.

flag.note: Under some injury/disease conditions, blood-derived cells can also enter the CNS; the resident population is yolk-sac-derived.

steps.prompt: Why does the CNS need its own resident immune cells rather than relying on blood-borne ones?
options: Because blood-borne immune cells are simply too small to be useful
The blood-brain barrier limits entry, so resident surveillance is needed
Because neurons themselves already act as the brain's immune cells
Because the brain has no immune needs and never faces infection
steps.explanation: The barrier that protects the CNS also limits routine immune access, so a built-in resident population (microglia) handles surveillance and first response.

steps.prompt: Microglia are often described as the CNS counterpart of which peripheral cell?
steps.explanation: Microglia are macrophage-like: resident, phagocytic, innate. The parallel helps you transfer macrophage logic (B1-L3) into the brain.

steps.setup: A researcher labels blood cells and finds that, in a healthy adult brain, almost none of the microglia carry the label.
steps.prompt: What does that suggest about microglial maintenance?
options: That microglia are replaced fresh from the blood every single day
That microglia are largely self-renewing residents, not blood-replaced
That microglia are actually neurons rather than immune cells
That the labeling method simply failed to work in this experiment
steps.reveal: Little blood-cell contribution in the healthy adult fits a self-renewing resident population, consistent with the yolk-sac origin story.

sources.note: Fate mapping: adult microglia derive from primitive (yolk-sac) macrophages.
